SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology04 / 25
Defining Race

Race stems from belief in shared common ancestry, based on biological traits;

A social construction based on some biological traits (mostly skin colors).

A quick re-cap: Social construction of reality theory argues that “what matters is not what it is, but what perceived to be”.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology05 / 25
A Brief History of Race

Human beings have always been categorizing themselves, but “race” only appeared in modern time.

In ancient times, people were more likely to be categorized according to religion, language, lineage, and geographical location. (e.g Ancient Greece)

From the 16th century, Europeans began to use three different categories  to classify the different groups of people they encountered through continental exploration: Mongoloid (Asians or “Yellow race”), Caucasoid (Europeans or “White race”), Negroid (Africans or “Black race”), and Australoid (Australian Aborigines).

From the very beginning, these terms convey a sense of superiority & inferiority based on socioeconomic power and technological advancement.

Yes, the racial differentiation is about power! It is in fact racial stratification.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology07 / 25
“Race” in the US Censuses

Census 1790: "White", "Slaves"

Census 1850: "White", "Black", "Mulatto"

Census 1890: "White," "Black," "Mulatto," "Quadroon," "Octoroon," "Chinese," "Japanese," or "Indian"

Census 1920: "White," "Black," "Mulatto," "Quadroon," "Octoroon," "Chinese," "Japanese," "Hindu", "Korean", and "Filipino"

Census 1930: “White,” “Negro,” “Indian,” "Chinese," "Japanese," "Hindu", "Korean", and "Filipino", "Mexican" (One-Drop-of-Blood Rule)

Census 1940: President Franklin D. Roosevelt promoted a "good neighbor" policy that sought better relations with Mexico. "Mexican" was classified as "White".

Census 1950: Removed “Hindu” and “Korean” from the race choices

Census 1960: Changed “Indian” to “American Indian”, as well as added “Hawaiian,” “Part-Hawaiian,” “Aleut,” and “Eskimo”.

Census 1970: Re-added “Korean”; East Indians (the term used at that time for people whose ancestry is from the Indian subcontinent) were counted as White.

Census 1980: Added Vietnamese, Indian (East), Guamanian, Samoan

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology08 / 25
Racial Classification from 2000 & 2010 & 2020 US Census

White – A person having origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East, or North Africa.

Black or African American – A person having origins in any of the Black racial groups of Africa.

American Indian or Alaska Native – A person having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America (including Central America) and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment.

Asian – A person having origins in any of the original peoples of the Far East, Southeast Asia, or the Indian subcontinent including, for example, Cambodia, China, India, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Pakistan, the Philippine Islands, Thailand, and Vietnam.

Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander – A person having origins in any of the original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, or other Pacific Islands.

Hispanic or Latino - A person of Cuban, Mexican, Puerto Rican, South or Central American, or other Spanish culture or origin regardless of race ("For this census, Hispanic origins are not races.")

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology09 / 25
“Race” in 2020 US Census: A Disclaimer

“The racial categories included in the census questionnaire generally reflect a social definition of race recognized in this country and not an attempt to define race biologically, anthropologically, or genetically. In addition, it is recognized that the categories of the race item include racial and national origin or sociocultural groups. People may choose to report more than one race to indicate their racial mixture, such as "American Indian" and "White." People who identify their origin as Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish may be of any race.”

A common pattern: The Color Terminology

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology10 / 25
An International Perspective

E.g.: In Australia, since the time of white settlement, governments have used no less than 67 classifications, descriptions or definitions to determine who is an Aboriginal person. Currently, they use a “three-part“ definition: An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander is a person of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent who identifies as an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and is accepted as such by the community in which he [or she] lives.

In Brazil, dozens of racial labels exist to classify people based on very specific combinations of skin color, hair color, hair texture, facial features, and so forth. Full siblings can be of different races.

In China/Japan/Korea, no such a thing as “race”

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology11 / 25
What is ethnicity?

Ethnicity stems from belief in shared common descent, based on cultural similarities;

Like race, it is also socially constructed

Symbolic Ethnicity: “a nationality, not in the sense of carrying the rights and duties of citizenship but identifying with a past or future nationality”

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology12 / 25
Slide 12

Comparing Race and Ethnicity

1. Race = socially constructed based on biological traits

2. Ethnicity = socially constructed based on cultural similarities

3. Race is anchored in biology and hierarchy terms; Ethnicity is anchored in culture and (sometimes) hierarchy terms.

4. Though seem to be self-identified , both Race and Ethnicity can be imposed on individuals.

Note, both are socially constructed and symbolic. But both are real!

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology16 / 25
Summary

Both Race and Ethnicity are Social Constructs

One based on perceived ancestry/biological traits, the other based on shared culture/language

The boundary between “race” and “ethnicity” could be fluid

Both form a mark that distinct/divides people, with the potential for leading to oppression and conflict.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology18 / 25
The Problem of Racism

Racism: prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against a person or people based on their membership in a particular racial or ethnic group.

Racial/ethnic Stereotype: an oversimplified set of beliefs about people classified as a certain race or ethnicity.

Racial/ethnic Prejudice: negative beliefs/attitudes held about individuals classified as a certain race or ethnicity;

Racial/ethnic Discrimination: any behavior/actions that involve unfair treatment of individuals classified as a certain race or ethnicity.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology20 / 25
Structural Racism

Embedded in laws, policies, and routinized practices of society that provide advantages to certain racial groups while disadvantaging others

Slavery in the U.S.

Jim Crow Law in the U.S.; Apartheid in South Africa

Today’s structural racism is more hidden (Racism without Racist) :

Discriminatory practices are rare (or explicitly forbidden) in laws, policies, and/or formal institutions

Established practices of society can result in a reality that is punitive/unjust for racial minorities (based on numerous decisions from numerous individuals who could hardly be identified as racists. E.g., Housing Segregation and Redlining in America: A Short History )

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology21 / 25
Structural Racism: the case of segregation

Blacks are more likely to living in disadvantaged neighborhoods that are segregated from White neighborhoods

There is not a centralized planner/authority that is responsible for such segregation (though the discriminatory housing/loaning policies did play a role historically)

Such racial segregation is sustained by numerous individuals’ decision-making within the constraints of historical legacy and current social system

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology22 / 25
Structural Racism: the case of segregation

The Socio-structural Formation of Black Ghettos

Industrialization, urbanization and the Great Migration

Racial residential segregation rose (to solve the “dual crisis” – “crisis of threat to whiteness” and “crisis of cheap labor shortage”)

Redlining: assessment of loan risks based on the race of the applicant and the racial composition of the neighborhood

Suburbanization, “The white flight”, and political isolation of the black ghetto-dwellers

Today, redlining practices are legally prohibited, but the unfair structure has already been formed and solidified.

How Zoning Laws Are Holding Back America's Cities

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology23 / 25
Cultural Racism

Cultural Racism: instillation of the ideology of inferiority in the values, language, imagery, symbols, and unstated assumptions of the larger society (prejudice, stereotyping, unconscious bias, internalization of racial beliefs).

(e.g., racial profiling: the act of suspecting or targeting a person on the basis of observed racial characteristics.)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology24 / 25
Cultural Racism: The case of internalization of bias

“When I grew up my parents would hate me hanging out with anyone Asian. I mean they would literally say, ‘Don’t hang out with them.’ I guess they have a preconception of them as being gang members. I don’t know. I never really asked them. Maybe it was the way my parents influenced me because the whole time I was with anyone Asian I just felt uneasy. I can’t stand Vietnamese people or just Asians in general.”

—Vietnamese American Interviewee

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology25 / 25
Cultural Racism: The case of Vigilant Coping

Vigilant Coping: Attempting to protect oneself from anticipated discrimination by continuously monitoring and modifying one’s behavior and surroundings

“It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others, of measuring one’s soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity.”

—W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folks (1989 [1903]:3)
